title: The Ledger's Truth
passages:
Ines swallowed the stale air and stepped into the dim corridor, the old ledger clutched like a lifeline. The pod‑four jumpsuit stood in the doorway, its visor reflecting the amber glow, the new ledger open on a blank page that seemed to pulse. 'You have the wrong name,' the figure said, voice flat as the metal floor, 'the first cost is not Ines but the one who signed the cost.' Ines lifted the worn page, the ink smudged but legible: 'Ines Halvard – first cost.' She read it aloud, the words echoing off the shelves, and felt the ledger shiver as if recognizing a true signature.

Mara's fingers were raw, the gap yawning wider with each gust of vacuum. The clamp's metal groan rose to a scream, the welds protesting the outward pressure. She shoved her elbow into the conduit junction again, the impact sending a shudder through the deck, and the rush against her palms eased just enough for her to plant her right foot on the steel lip. 'Hold,' she muttered, teeth clenched, as the clamp began to bend, the metal stretching beyond its design limit.

Ines stepped forward, placed the old page on the ledger's blank spread, and pressed her thumb against the paper, the contact rule flashing in her mind. The figure watched, then nodded, and the ledger filled itself with a new line: 'Halvard, Ines – first cost.' The count on the gauge dropped a fraction, the loop reset, and the vacuum hissed as the bay began to equalize, buying the crew the seconds they needed.

Mara’s clamp gave up with a screech that rattled her teeth. The welded seam peeled back, the gap widened, and vacuum screamed into the bay. She jerked her hands free, palms blistered, and threw herself against the cycle door. “It’s not holding,” she said. “Get the valve.”

Jax threw his shoulder into the purge valve wheel. “It won’t seat,” he shouted. “Not without the bypass.”

Ines looked at the old page. *Halvard, Ines – first cost.* The shelf hadn’t been wrong. It had been waiting. She stepped to the bare metal port on the conduit junction—Tam Acker’s palm had logged there once—and pressed her burned hand flat against the cold plate. “Lira Kessler,” she said.

The port hummed. The gauge stopped falling. The amber light above the purge bay cycled to steady green, and the outward groan in the walls dropped to a murmur. The ledger in the pod-four figure’s hand snapped shut with a sound like a gavel. The figure turned its visor to Ines and said, “Cost accepted.”

The worn page grew warm. The ink slid, wet and fresh, and beneath her own name a second line appeared: *Ryla – unlogged mass.*

The ink was still wet on Ryla's name when Malik came through the hatch at a dead run, one hand raised, a strip of paper pinched between his fingers. "Don't let it close," he said. "The audit isn't a debt, it's a *list*. I annotated the true first name—" The bell struck. Amber light swallowed the bay, the comms died with a click, and the ink on his strip crawled like something alive, letters sliding into a new order. His mouth kept shaping the word, but the bell's note swallowed it whole.

The pod-four figure waited until the last note faded. Then it lifted the visor. Lira Kessler looked out at them, frost-burned along one cheek, eyes rimmed red. "You're late," she said. "You're always late." Ines felt the old page go cold in her hand. "You were the first cost." "I signed the invitation," Lira said. "I invited the author. I thought it would write us a rescue." She looked at the blank ledger. "It writes what it's paid to write. The cost is the fee." "Then unsign it." "The page doesn't take erasures." Lira's gaze moved to the green light above the bay. "And it doesn't remember you. Not after the bell."

The green light flickered. Went amber. The gauge needle, which had held steady for eleven seconds, began to fall. Somewhere behind the bulkhead, the clamp's broken seam groaned as the pressure found it again. Malik looked at his strip. The ink had settled into a single line: *Reyes, Malik – annotation rejected.* He laughed, short and ugly. "Well. That's me told."

Ines turned the old page over. The back was blank, but the paper was warm. She pressed her burned thumb to it and thought about what a new writer would read. "We don't write on the page," she said. "We write on the door." Lira's eyes narrowed. "There is no where." "There's steel." Ines bent and picked up a curl of the clamp's peeled seam, the metal still warm from the pressure. "Malik, get Mara off the door. Jax, the valve. If the next writer wants a cost, it can come read it off the hull."

Behind them, the ledger snapped open on its own. A new line wrote itself in wet black ink: *Halvard, Ines – first cost. Reyes, Malik – second.*

The ink from the new line dried into a faint sheen, and the ledger snapped shut with a finality that made Ines wince. “Well,” Malik said, rubbing his chin. “We’re now officially the most expensive crew in the system. First cost, second cost—soon we’ll need a budget.” Mara, still pressed against the cycle door, glanced back, her blistered hands tight on the clamp shard. “At least we’re not invisible.” Jax knocked the valve wheel once, the metal sighing under his grip. “If the next writer wants a price, let ‘em read it off the hull.” Ines stepped toward the purge bay door, the steel cold beneath her palm.

The surface was already scored with slender letters, faint but unmistakable: *Ines – first cost*, written in her own hand from a previous loop. She traced the letters with a fingertip, feeling the ridges. “They already wrote me in,” she said, voice dry. “Now we add the rest.” She seized the clamp shard, scratching a new line beside the old: *Ines – first cost. Malik – second. Door breached.* The gauge, which had been creeping down, halted its fall for a heartbeat, the amber light steadied to green, and the groan in the walls softened. But the relief was brief; a distant chime signaled the next bell’s approach, and the ledger in Lira’s pod‑four figure slid open once more, ready for a fresh name.

The chime sang, a thin, high note that made the station’s ribs ring, and the amber light above the purge bay flared one last time before cycling to green. Ines felt the old page go cold in her hand, the memory of the bell already fading, but the steel door still glittered with the words she and Malik had scratched: *Ines – first cost. Malik – second. Door breached*. She traced the ridges with a fingertip, feeling the warmth still thrumming from the clamp’s recent pressure.

‘Well,’ Malik said, rubbing his chin. ‘We’ve got ourselves a ledger full of expensive names. Might as well keep the trend.’ He grinned, a flash of teeth in the dim light. Mara, still leaning against the cycle door, wiped a smudge of grease from her blistered palm and added, ‘We already wrote ourselves in. Might as well finish the set.’ Jax knocked the valve wheel once, the metal sighing under his grip. ‘If the next writer wants a price, let ‘em read it off the hull.’

Ines seized a shard of the clamp’s peeled seam, dipped it in the faint ink residue that clung to the steel, and scratched a new line beside the old: *Ines – first cost. Malik – second. Door breached. Jax – third, valve turning*. The ink dried into a sheen, the amber light steadied to green, and a distant groan in the walls softened—but the relief was brief. The ledger in Lira’s pod‑four figure slid open once more, the fresh name already waiting: *Torin, Jax – third cost*.

The bell’s echo faded, and the gauge, now hovering just above the red zone, held steady, the crew exchanging glances of grim satisfaction. They had written themselves into the story, and the next writer would have to reckon with the cost they’d left on the hull.
